plan.title: Airlines Make More From Your Credit Card Than Flying
alt_titles: Your Airline Miles Are a Bad Deal (Here's Why)
Airlines Are Banks That Happen to Fly Planes
plan.description:
Delta got $8.2 billion from American Express in 2025, more than its operating profit. This is how airline credit cards and frequent flyer miles became the real business behind US airlines, why the points were once worth more than the planes, and why I think miles are now a bad deal for most people.

How airlines make money from credit cards, loyalty programs and miles: from American's 1981 phone-number trick to the $24 billion airlines borrowed against their programs in 2020-21.

Chapters:
0:00 Intro
0:55 The phone number trick
2:15 Enter the banks
3:45 Worth more than the airline
5:05 You're the collateral
6:05 Moving the goalposts
7:40 Who really pays
9:00 The verdict

segments.narration: Last year, Delta Air Lines got eight point two billion dollars from one company. And not for flying anyone anywhere.
The money came from American Express. It was paying for miles.
By Delta's own adjusted numbers, that's about one and a half times what the whole airline made in operating profit.

visual.label: Amex cash vs. Delta's operating profit

segments.narration: American Airlines is even stranger. Its card and loyalty partners paid it six point two billion dollars.
That's roughly four times its operating profit.
So if an airline makes more from your credit card than from your flight... is it still an airline?
A consumer advocate put it bluntly to Reuters this year.
He said the modern airline is a gigantic rewards program that just happens to fly airplanes.

visual.text: The modern airline is a gigantic *rewards program* that just happens to fly airplanes.

segments.narration: And if you have ever swiped a card to earn miles, you're part of that business. Maybe more than you think.
Because the deal you signed up for has been shrinking. One industry study says the value you get back for your loyalty has fallen by about half since 2019.
I think frequent flyer miles have become a bad deal for most people. By the end, you can decide if I'm right.
To see how we got here, we have to go back to 1981. And to a list of phone numbers.
In 1978, America deregulated its airlines. Carriers could suddenly fight over routes and prices, and they did.
Airlines needed a way to stop people from just booking whoever was cheapest that day.
Texas International tried a frequent flyer scheme first, in 1979. American Airlines turned the idea into a machine.
Its trick was clever. It searched its SABRE booking computer for phone numbers that kept showing up again and again.
Every repeat number was a frequent traveler. It found about a hundred and thirty thousand of them.

visual.label: Frequent flyers found by phone number

segments.narration: Add sixty thousand airport lounge members, and AAdvantage launched on May first, 1981, with about a hundred and ninety thousand people already enrolled.
The pitch was simple. Fly with us, collect miles, earn a free trip.
Within days, United launched its own program. Soon every big airline had one.
And almost from the start, the airline could change the rules. In 1988, American ran triple-mile promotions, then raised the number of miles you needed for a reward.
A year later, in 1989, miles started to expire.
Still, for years, that's mostly what miles were. A thank-you for flying a lot.
Then the banks showed up.
Here's the move that changed everything. Airlines started selling their miles to other companies.
A bank puts the airline's name on a credit card. Every time you buy groceries with it, the bank buys miles from the airline and passes them to you.
The airline gets cash today. You get a promise of a seat someday.
Jay Sorensen, a consultant who has studied these programs for years, told the New York Times exactly where the shift came from.
What really changed the dynamics of these programs, he said, is the arrival of credit cards.

visual.text: What really changed the dynamics of these programs is the arrival of *credit cards*.

segments.narration: And remember, the airline decides how many miles it creates, and how many miles a seat will cost.
The biggest of these deals is between Delta and American Express.
In 2024, people spent about a hundred and eighty-six billion dollars on Delta-branded cards.
That's roughly one dollar in every eight spent on American Express cards anywhere in the world.

visual.label:
of all Amex card spending
on Delta cards

segments.narration: Delta got seven point four billion dollars from Amex that year. Then eight point two billion the next. Its executives have talked about reaching ten billion.
To put that in proportion, the Amex money alone is about fourteen percent of Delta's adjusted revenue. From one partner.
And these programs are enormous. By 2020, MileagePlus had more than a hundred million members. By 2021, AAdvantage had over a hundred and fifteen million.
That's more members than most countries have people.
And here's what makes this money so special. It's steady. When people stop flying, they keep shopping.
In the 2008 recession, United's overall revenue fell nineteen percent. Its loyalty revenue fell just two percent.
So which is worth more: the planes, or the points? In 2020, the whole world found out.
In the spring of 2020, the pandemic emptied the sky.
Planes sat parked in rows. Airlines were losing money every single day, and they needed loans.
Lenders want collateral. Something valuable they can take if you can't pay.
In June 2020, United took out a five billion dollar loan, backed by its MileagePlus program.
The idea wasn't brand new. Colombia's Avianca had borrowed against its LifeMiles program back in 2017. But nobody had done it at this size.
And United had something lenders loved. Its card deals with Chase and Visa had just been extended into 2029. Years of guaranteed swiping.
In its own filing, United valued MileagePlus at about twenty-one point nine billion dollars.
At the time, the whole of United Airlines on the stock market, every plane and route included, was worth around eleven point seven billion.
Let that sink in. The points program was worth almost twice the airline that owns it.
Delta went next. In September 2020, it borrowed nine billion dollars against SkyMiles. It had planned six and a half. Lenders wanted more.
Look at how Delta set it up. The loan went through a brand new company in the Cayman Islands, called SkyMiles IP.
At the time, credit agencies rated Delta's debt as junk. Yet it borrowed against SkyMiles at four and a half to four point seven five percent.
My read is simple. The lenders weren't betting on the airline. They were betting on the miles.
And the miles held up. Even in that terrible year, SkyMiles brought in two point nine billion dollars in the first nine months of 2020.

visual.label: SkyMiles income, Jan–Sept 2020
visual.sub: in the worst year in modern aviation

segments.narration: Then in March 2021, American raised ten billion dollars backed by AAdvantage, and used it to pay back a loan from the US Treasury.
That's twenty-four billion dollars, borrowed against miles, by just three airlines.
But what exactly were the lenders getting? Partly... you.
Delta's loan documents spell out what backs the deal.
The rights to its credit card partnerships and the payments from them. The bank accounts where SkyMiles money lands.
And the program's intellectual property, including member profile data.
In plain words, the program and the information on its members, you included, helped secure a nine billion dollar loan.
That's why the airline cares so much that you keep swiping.
United's numbers show how lopsided it is. In 2019, MileagePlus brought in five point three billion dollars in cash.
Seventy-one percent of that came from outside partners, like card issuers. Not from people buying flights on United.
Think about what that means. Most of the money in the program has nothing to do with sitting on a plane.
There is one catch for the airline. Every mile it sells is a seat it owes someone, someday.
By late 2020, Delta's loyalty deferred revenue, basically miles sold but not yet flown, stood at seven point one billion dollars.
That's an IOU to millions of members. So what's the cheapest way to shrink an IOU?
You make each mile worth a little less. And when you hold a promise, the person who wrote it can rewrite it.
American already showed the way. In 2016, it stopped giving miles for the distance you flew, and started giving them for the price of your ticket.
So a cheap long flight suddenly earned a lot less. In 2022, it replaced its elite rules again, with something called Loyalty Points.
Then, in September 2023, Delta went further, with big changes to SkyMiles.
Elite status would no longer come from how much you flew. It would come from how much you spent.
The top tier, Diamond, used to need twenty thousand qualifying dollars, plus enough flights. The new plan said thirty-five thousand.
Lounge visits for people holding Delta's premium cards were going to be capped too.
Customers revolted. Within two weeks, Delta's chief executive Ed Bastian admitted the changes probably went too far.
In October, Delta backed off. Diamond came down to twenty-eight thousand. Still far above where it started.
And it's not just Delta. That industry study found that several airlines have cut or ended mileage earning on their cheapest tickets.
Which is a big part of why the value you get back has fallen by about half.
Regulators noticed. In September 2024, the US Department of Transportation opened a probe into the reward programs of the four biggest US airlines.

shots.image: United States Department of Transportation headquarters

segments.narration: It named four worries. Points losing value. Hidden and changing prices. Extra fees. And less competition.
Investigators asked the airlines for records on how their programs had changed over the past six years.
The stated goal was to make sure people get the value they were promised.

visual.text: Our goal is to ensure consumers are getting the *value that was promised* to them.

segments.narration: Pete Buttigieg, the Transportation Secretary at the time, summed up the problem.
He said these rewards are controlled by a company that can unilaterally change their value.

visual.text: These rewards are controlled by a company that can *unilaterally change their value*.

segments.narration: To be fair, a probe is not a verdict. Nobody has been found guilty of anything. But it shows how this deal looks from the outside.
So if you don't have an airline card, none of this touches you. Right? Not quite.
Every time a shop takes a card, the shop pays a fee. And there's a fight in Congress over those fees.
Supporters of a bill known as Durbin-Marshall say more competition between card networks would cut costs for merchants. The airlines' trade group warned it could put airline card rewards at risk.
When an industry fights that hard over a swipe fee, it tells you where the money is.
Now, the other side. Plenty of people love these cards. Lounge access, free bags, upgrades.
Alaska Airlines' loyalty chief told Reuters that people without a card still earn meaningful value just by flying.

visual.text: Non-cardholders continue to earn *meaningful value* through flying.
visual.who: Kevin Scott, Alaska Airlines (paraphrased by Reuters)

segments.narration: And if you fly a lot, pay your card off every month, and book carefully, the math can work for you.
But I don't think that's most people. The way the system works, the airline comes out ahead almost any way you play it.
Carry a balance on the card? The bank earns interest. Your miles sit unused? The airline already has the cash. The price of a free seat goes up? You need more miles.
Delta, for example, books part of that Amex cash as revenue right away. The rest waits until you actually spend your miles.
One loyalty expert told the New York Times what would happen if you took these programs away.

visual.tag: Evert de Boer · On Point Loyalty

segments.narration: He said it would have a huge impact on the big US carriers.

visual.text: If you were to take away the loyalty programs, it would have a *huge impact* on the big U.S. carriers.
visual.who: Evert de Boer, On Point Loyalty

segments.narration: So, is your airline really a bank that flies planes?
Here's what the numbers say. Delta gets more from Amex than it makes in operating profit. American's partners pay it about four times its profit.
And it's spreading. At Alaska Airlines, loyalty is now about sixteen percent of all revenue. Southwest sells most of its points to JPMorgan Chase.
This year, Reuters reports, rising jet fuel costs tied to the Middle East conflict are squeezing airline margins. Which makes the steady card money matter even more.
And in 2020, United's points program was valued at almost twice the airline itself.
My verdict: miles aren't a gift. They're a currency the airline creates, and the airline sets the exchange rate.
So treat them like one. Spend them, don't hoard them. Don't chase status you can't afford. And never carry a balance for a free flight.
Because in this business, the plane is what they show you. The card is what they sell you.
If you want to see the same playbook on the ground, watch how Costco really makes money next. It isn't the groceries either.
